findings.message: Option c is self-refuting on its face: it claims the 5-minute TTL expires "because low-effort turns finish too quickly", yet faster turns shorten the gap between requests, as its own "why" concedes. No learner reasoning about TTL would select it, so it adds no discrimination.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a plausible cache-invalidation confound, e.g. "The harness rewrites the system prompt to describe the current effort mode, so the prefix text differs between turns." and set its why to explain that the observed misses track the effort parameter itself, not a prompt edit.

findings.message: Option C states exactly the same remediation as the keyed option A ("Remove the filter so the assistant turn, including its thinking and redacted_thinking blocks, is sent back exactly as the API returned it"), only adding a runbook note, which is documentation rather than a change to the request. Both options therefore fix the 400 and a careful learner cannot pick a single intended answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C with the distractor its "why" actually describes, e.g. "Disable extended thinking for the agent so no thinking or redacted_thinking blocks are produced."

findings.message: Option C's "why" ("changes model behaviour and cost across the whole application, and on models where thinking is always on the request fails with another 400") explains why disabling extended thinking is wrong; it has nothing to do with C's actual text about removing the filter and recording it in a runbook.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the "why" with the option text after C is rewritten, or if C stays as-is, explain that it is identical to the minimal fix plus extra unnecessary work.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks how Messages API streaming works (SSE over HTTP, not WebSockets) and when the SDK requires streaming, but the answer text describes the distinction between client-executed tools and Anthropic server tools. A learner would come away with no correct answer to the question asked (and would be led to think the tool-execution split is the answer), while the code snippet and realWorldUsage note both concern SSE streaming.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the streaming answer, e.g.: "There is no WebSocket endpoint. The Messages API streams with server-sent events over a normal HTTPS POST (stream: true), emitting message_start, content_block_start/delta/stop, message_delta and message_stop events; the SDK's client.messages.stream() helper wraps this and exposes text_stream plus get_final_message(). Streaming is mandatory (the SDK/API rejects or warns on a non-streaming request) once the request's expected generation time is long — e.g. very large max_tokens such as 64000 on a long-running model request — because a single non-streamed response would exceed the request timeout. Proxy the SSE stream to the browser as-is." Keep the tool client-vs-server text for a separate card.

findings.message: The keyed answer is option c ("Wait for requests to start failing after retirement"), which is factually wrong and whose own "why" text explains why it is wrong; the explanation and the option "why" fields all identify option a (Console usage export plus the at-least-60-day notice) as the correct approach, but option a is marked "correct": false. The keying is inverted, so a learner is taught that waiting for outages is the MOST reliable approach.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a and "correct": false on option c, leave option a's "why" as null (or explain the key), and keep c's existing "why" as the distractor rationale.

findings.message: The explanation states a specific size guideline ("targeted under 200 lines per file") for CLAUDE.md that is not a documented limit or official recommendation — Anthropic's guidance is qualitative (keep it concise and human-readable). This unverified number should be re-checked against current documentation before publishing.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace "targeted under 200 lines per file" with non-numeric guidance, e.g. "kept short and human-readable, since it is prepended to every session's context".

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is copied verbatim from the first sentence of the explanation, so it hands the learner one of the four required mappings (CSV → built-in code execution server tool) before they answer, plus the general decision rule for built-in tools.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the hint from the question, or replace it with a non-answering cue such as "Hint: consider who runs the capability, who owns the logic, whether it is knowledge or an external system, and how many apps need it."

findings.message: The parenthetical "default 30-second timeout" for a type "prompt" hook is a specific numeric default that differs from the documented 60-second default for command hooks; it is peripheral to the answer and should be verified against current Claude Code hooks documentation before publishing.
findings.suggestedFix: Either drop the parenthetical or confirm the current documented default timeout for prompt hooks, e.g. "a type \"prompt\" hook (subject to its own configurable timeout) sends the hook input to a Claude model for a single-turn decision".

findings.message: "Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1)" is not a real Claude model or model ID — the Claude family uses the Haiku/Sonnet/Opus tiers, and no "Fable" tier exists; the card also internally conflicts by placing this invented model above Opus 5 in price while describing Opus 5 as the model for "complex agentic coding and enterprise work".
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the "Claude Fable 5.1 / claude-fable-5-1" entry and list only the real current models (e.g. Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Haiku 4.5) with IDs and prices taken from the current models overview page.

findings.message: The stated Opus 5 price of $5/$25 per million input/output tokens should be re-verified: the Opus tier has historically been priced far higher ($15/$75), so this figure is the most likely to be wrong or stale and it is the centre of the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check Opus 5 input/output pricing (and the $2/$10 Sonnet 5 and $1/$5 Haiku 4.5 figures) against the current Anthropic pricing page and correct them.

findings.message: The card packs highly volatile data (IDs, prices, context/output limits, effort defaults, retirement dates) into one answer with source: null, so nothing in it can be verified and the imminent Haiku 4.5 retirement date (October 15, 2026, three weeks after the review date) cannot be trusted.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a source with a quote from the Anthropic models overview / pricing / deprecations pages, or split the card so each volatile figure is individually sourced.

findings.message: The stem's "Hint" quotes the opening words of the keyed option verbatim ("Mark the rulebook with a one-hour cache_control block, submit a ..."), so a learner with no knowledge of prompt caching can match the hint to option c by surface string alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint line from the question stem: "A weekly batch of 60,000 requests shares a 30,000-token rulebook. Cache hit rates hover near 20% because requests are processed concurrently in arbitrary order. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to raise hits?"

findings.message: Option b's "why" gives a fabricated rationale: max_tokens must be at least 1 in every Messages API call (batch or synchronous), so it is not "rejected inside a batch" for expiry reasons, and there is no max_tokens=0 pre-warm mechanism in the synchronous API either. Re-check this claim against current documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite b's why as: "max_tokens must be at least 1, so there is no zero-token pre-warm request in any Anthropic API; a cache-seeding request has to actually run and complete before the dependent requests are submitted."

findings.message: Option d is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option a ("Move the contract to the top of the prompt inside <document> tags and put the question as the last line.") prefixed with "Adopt this approach:", so two options state the same correct change while only a is keyed; a careful learner cannot pick one answer. Option d's "why" also argues about a larger context window, which its text never mentions, indicating the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore option d to the distractor its rationale describes, e.g. "Switch to a model with a 1M-token context window and resend the prompt unchanged."

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"Create a CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions from the management ...\"", which quotes the opening of option A verbatim, so a learner with no AWS knowledge can pick the key by string matching alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint:" sentence from the question stem so the learner must reason from the requirements (multi-account/multi-Region deployment, auto-enrollment of new accounts, drift visibility).

findings.message: Option C (Elastic Beanstalk to create an environment per account containing the baseline) is implausible to the point that no learner would consider it — Beanstalk deploys application environments and has no mechanism for CloudTrail/Config/GuardDuty/IAM baselines across accounts.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C with a plausible near-miss, e.g. "Create a CloudFormation StackSet with self-managed permissions, create the execution roles in each account, and deploy the template to an explicit list of account IDs and Regions" (fails the auto-enrollment requirement).

findings.message: Option D is a verbatim duplicate of keyed option A ("Point the reporting application at the cluster's reader endpoint and attach an Aurora Auto Scaling policy...") but is keyed false, so two identically-worded options are correct and the learner cannot pick a single answer. Its "why" also discusses RDS Proxy, which the option text never mentions.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option D's text with the RDS Proxy distractor its "why" describes, e.g. "Put an RDS Proxy in front of the cluster and point the reporting application at the proxy endpoint."

findings.message: The explanation rebuts distractors that do not exist on this card — it names an "instance endpoint" option as "the distractor" and also dismisses an RDS Multi-AZ standby option, neither of which appears among options A–D.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim the explanation to address only the options actually presented (reader endpoint + Auto Scaling, cluster endpoint, vertical scaling of the writer, RDS Proxy), or add the instance-endpoint option it references.

findings.message: Option C's text is a verbatim duplicate of the keyed option A (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), so two options state the same correct solution and a learner cannot pick a single answer; C's "why" text describes AWS Global Accelerator, indicating the intended option text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C's text with the Global Accelerator option its "why" describes, e.g. "Put the bucket behind AWS Global Accelerator so viewers reach it over the AWS backbone through static anycast IPs."

findings.message: The explanation credits Rekognition with detecting "printed and handwritten text"; Rekognition's DetectText/DetectTextInVideo is documented for scene text (printed/typed) in images and video, while handwriting extraction is an Amazon Textract capability — the same distinction the card draws at the end. The author should verify this claim against current Rekognition documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "printed and handwritten text" to "text in scenes and images (e.g., signs, street text)" and keep handwriting/forms/tables attributed to Textract.

findings.message: The `allowed-tools` line in the code snippet uses invalid permission-rule syntax: Claude Code expects a comma-separated list and a colon before the wildcard (e.g. `Bash(git tag:*)`), not space-separated entries with `Bash(git tag *)`. As written the rules would not match the intended commands, so the snippet teaches broken syntax.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the frontmatter line to: `allowed-tools: Bash(git tag:*), Bash(gh release:*)`

findings.message: The explanation's claim that the description is "truncated at 1,536 characters together with when_to_use" should be re-verified: the documented SKILL.md frontmatter uses kebab-case fields (name, description, allowed-tools) and a different description length limit, and `when_to_use` is not a Claude Code skill field.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the current Agent Skills / Claude Code documentation for the exact description character limit and drop or correct the `when_to_use` reference (e.g. state only "the description is loaded at startup and is subject to a documented length limit").

findings.message: The card states that name, description, and input_schema are the three *required* fields of a user-defined tool. In the Anthropic Messages API tool schema only `name` and `input_schema` are required; `description` is optional (though strongly recommended), and a request with a tool that omits it is accepted.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "A user-defined tool has two required fields — name (must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$) and input_schema (a JSON Schema object) — plus description, which is optional but strongly recommended..." and adjust the question to "What fields make up a user-defined tool..." rather than "the three required fields".

findings.message: The quantitative and scope claims about input_examples (roughly 20–50 tokens per simple example, 100–200 for complex nested ones, 400 on an invalid example, not accepted on server tools or the computer/browser toolsets) are specific and unsourced; they should be re-verified against current tool-use documentation before publishing.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a source (url + quote) from the current tool-use / input_examples documentation backing the token-cost ranges, the 400 validation behavior, and the server-tool/computer-and-browser-toolset exclusions, or drop the unverified numbers.

findings.message: The card keys option b (duplicate stack in a second Region with Route 53 failover) as correct, but the explanation, the qualifier "MOST cost-effective", and option b's own "why" text all state that a second Region is the wrong, overspending answer; the correct answer is option a (add subnets in additional Availability Zones to the Auto Scaling group and enable them on the ALB). As keyed, the card teaches a false answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a and "correct": false on option b; move option b's current "why" text to remain as its distractor rationale and set option a's "why" to null (or an explanation of why it is right).

findings.message: Option b's "why" states gp3 "tops out at 16,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s per volume"; the documented gp3 per-volume maximum throughput is 1,000 MiB/s, so the 2,000 MiB/s figure appears wrong (it does not affect the key, since the 16,000 IOPS ceiling already disqualifies gp3).
findings.suggestedFix: Change the why to "gp3 tops out at 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s per volume and offers single-digit millisecond latency, so it can reach neither 120,000 IOPS nor the sub-millisecond target." after re-checking the current gp3 maximums in the EBS volume types documentation.

findings.message: The card asserts a hard API restriction — "Non-default temperature returns a 400 on Sonnet 5" / "Temperature is rejected on 4.7 and later models" — which is a strong, specific claim about parameter validation that should be verified against current API documentation; the rest of distractor B's rejection (added randomness reduces format consistency) stands on its own regardless.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the temperature restriction against the current Messages API docs for Sonnet 5. If non-default temperature is merely discouraged or only restricted with extended thinking/top_p, reword to e.g. "Temperature is constrained on current models and higher randomness makes the layout less consistent, not more."

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST cost-effective", but nothing in the card differentiates the options on cost — the explanation and every "why" argue enforcement/security (allowlisting, CLAUDE.md is not enforcement, classifier is not an exact allowlist). Option B (--dangerously-skip-permissions) would arguably be at least as "cost-effective" since it never blocks or retries, so the stated qualifier does not select the key; the deciding criterion is actually strict enforcement of the allowlist.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the qualifier with one that matches the reasoning, e.g. change the stem to "Which invocation MOST strictly enforces the requirement while letting the job run unattended?" and set mcq.qualifier to "MOST strictly enforces the allowlist".

findings.message: The stem asks "what do you change?" for consumers offline for a week, but the explanation only says to "raise it when consumers lag" without naming the concrete setting and value (MessageRetentionPeriod must be raised above the 4-day default to at least 7 days / 604800 seconds, up to the 14-day maximum), so the card never fully answers its own question.
findings.suggestedFix: Amend the first sentence to something like: "SQS keeps a message for 4 days by default; retention runs from 60 seconds to 14 days, so set MessageRetentionPeriod to at least 604800 seconds (7 days) — commonly the 14-day maximum — to survive a week-long consumer outage."

findings.message: The size-cap sentence is garbled ("256 KB for years, and the figure exam questions still use, and that is still the current quota"), which obscures the claim being taught; the author should also re-verify against current SQS quotas that 256 KB is still the maximum message size.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "Bodies have a hard cap of 256 KB (the figure exam questions still use, and still the current quota)."

findings.message: The keyed answer is option C ("Attach a second virtual private gateway to the VPC"), which is factually wrong and is contradicted by both the card's own explanation and option C's own "why" text (only one VGW per VPC, and the failure was customer-side). The correct design is option A (second customer gateway device + second VPN connection to the same VGW with BGP), which is left unkeyed and has a null "why".
findings.suggestedFix: Move "correct": true from option C to option A, leave option A's "why" as null, and keep option C's existing "why" as its distractor rationale.

findings.message: Option b is verbatim the keyed option a plus "Record the change in the team's runbook," so it is equally correct (and equally cost-effective) and a learner cannot choose between a and b. Its "why" text and the explanation both describe an hourly manual snapshot option that does not appear in the choices, indicating the option text was replaced in error.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option b's text with the distractor its "why" and the explanation describe, e.g. "Take hourly manual snapshots of the instance and retain them for 30 days."

findings.message: The explanation calls the parent product "Amazon Quick"; the announced product name is "Amazon Quick Suite" (with Quick Sight as its BI capability), so the name as written is incomplete/incorrect and should be re-checked against current AWS documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Change "the business intelligence feature of Amazon Quick and the successor of QuickSight" to "the business intelligence capability of Amazon Quick Suite and the successor to Amazon QuickSight".

findings.message: Option f ("AWS Glue ETL jobs written to answer each ad hoc query") is implausible enough that essentially no learner would select it — nobody would author a batch ETL job per interactive question — so it adds no discrimination to the item.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option f with a plausible interactive-query alternative, e.g. "Amazon Redshift Serverless for both teams, copying the S3 files into the warehouse before every ad hoc query", and give it a "why" noting the needless load step for occasional queries.

findings.message: Option c's text is a verbatim duplicate of keyed option b ("Submit the notes through the Message Batches API as two batches of at most 100,000 requests, keyed by custom_id...") but is marked incorrect, so two identical options are presented and the learner cannot pick a single answer. Option c's "why" discusses prompt caching, showing the intended distractor text was lost in a copy-paste.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c's text with the prompt-caching distractor its "why" describes, e.g. "Keep the synchronous Messages API but add a cache_control breakpoint to the classification prompt so the shared prefix is served from the prompt cache."

findings.message: The stem's distinctive requirement "validate the totals in code before anything downstream runs" is echoed only in the keyed option ("a programmatic totals check as the gate"); no other option mentions any code/programmatic check, so a learner who knows nothing about workflows vs. agents can match the wording and pick (a) without engaging the concept being tested.
findings.suggestedFix: Give the distractors comparable surface coverage of the code gate, e.g. (b) "An autonomous agent with tool access, including a totals-validation tool, that plans the step order itself for each invoice" and (c) "An orchestrator LLM that calls a totals-validation worker plus four other workers in an order it chooses per invoice".

findings.message: The keyed option's count is internally inconsistent with the stem: of the five steps, only four (extract, classify, draft, translate) are LLM calls — the totals validation is explicitly a code step — so "five sequential LLM calls and a programmatic totals check" implies six steps.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword the key as "A prompt-chaining workflow with four sequential LLM calls and a programmatic totals check as the gate after the extraction step."

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" line is a verbatim copy of the explanation's first sentence, so it hands the learner the entire production-side answer (reserved DB instance, 1/3-year commitment, what is and is not discounted) before they answer, leaving only the stop-behaviour trap to recall.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the hint or replace it with a non-answer nudge, e.g. "Hint: think about commitment-based pricing for steady workloads and what RDS does to a stopped instance over time."

findings.message: "For longer gaps take a snapshot and delete it" is ambiguous — "it" most naturally attaches to the snapshot, which would be the opposite of the intended advice (delete the DB instance and keep the snapshot).
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "For longer gaps, take a manual snapshot and delete the DB instance, then restore from the snapshot when needed."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks what changed in thinking/reasoning display between Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Sonnet 5 and what the display options are (as of 2026-09), but the answer text is entirely about discouraging markdown and eliciting flowing prose. A learner is given content that does not address — and therefore misstates — the keyed topic, and the stem's second half ("what are the display options") is never answered.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with one that answers the stem: state what changed in the reasoning output for Sonnet 5 (e.g. the default thinking display for the new model), enumerate the supported display values (such as the "summarized" value shown in the code snippet plus the other permitted modes), and explain why an unset display leaves the reasoning panel empty while token cost is unchanged.

findings.message: The explanation names "Claude Fable 5.1", a model that does not exist and that is inconsistent with the models in the stem (Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 5); this appears to be leftover text from a different card.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the "Claude Fable 5.1" sentence, or replace the model name with the model actually under discussion (Claude Sonnet 5) once the explanation is rewritten to match the stem.

findings.message: The code snippet ({"thinking": {"type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized"}}) is never referenced or explained by the answer text, so the field names and values ("adaptive", "summarized") are unverified against the rest of the card.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the thinking block's type/display field names and permitted values against current API documentation, and have the rewritten explanation walk through the snippet explicitly.

findings.message: Option D discloses its own defect in the option text ("without creating permission sets or account assignments"), so no learner would select it; it tests reading rather than knowledge of cross-account access.
findings.suggestedFix: Make D a plausible complete-sounding alternative, e.g. "Enable IAM Identity Center and create permission sets assigned to the engineers for the dev and prod accounts" — and have the "why" explain that this replaces, rather than connects, the existing IAM users in the identity account.

findings.message: The answer is backwards: S3 Lifecycle rejects the day-7 Standard-IA transition, not the day-20 step. PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration validates that a transition to STANDARD_IA (or ONEZONE_IA) specifies at least 30 days ("'Days' in Transition action must be greater than or equal to 30 for storageClass 'STANDARD_IA'"), so the explanation's claim that "Moving to Standard-IA at day 7 alone is valid" is false. The day-20 Deep Archive step is also invalid, but only because it is less than 30 days after the (already illegal) IA transition.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the answer: S3 rejects the day 7 transition to Standard-IA because a lifecycle transition to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA must be at least 30 days after object creation; in addition, when both transitions are in one rule the Glacier Deep Archive transition must be at least 30 days after the Standard-IA transition (e.g. day 30 to Standard-IA, day 60 or later to Deep Archive).

findings.message: The explanation states the 90-day (Glacier Flexible Retrieval) and 180-day (Deep Archive) figures as lifecycle-transition scheduling constraints. These are billing minimum storage durations, not limits that block a subsequent transition being scheduled; the only scheduling constraints S3 validates are the 30-day minimum for IA classes and the 30-day gap between an IA transition and a Glacier/Deep Archive transition in the same rule.
findings.suggestedFix: Distinguish the two concepts: list 90/180 days as minimum billable storage durations (early-deletion charges) and keep the 30-day rules as the lifecycle validation constraints.

findings.message: This is a question-and-answer card ("mcq": null), but the explanation ends with "The distractor blames the day 7 IA step or accepts the rule unchanged" — a leftover reference to multiple-choice options the learner never sees (and which in fact names the correct answer).
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the final sentence about the distractor.

findings.message: The realWorldUsage note claims "For a brand-new VPC, a regional NAT gateway expands across zones on its own." AWS NAT gateways are zonal resources created in a specific subnet/AZ; there is no regional NAT gateway that spans AZs, and this directly contradicts the card's own explanation that "A NAT gateway is redundant only inside its own zone."
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "A NAT gateway is always zonal, so any VPC design needs one gateway per Availability Zone plus a per-subnet route table pointing at the local gateway — the extra gateway alone is not enough."

findings.message: The explanation's closing sentence, "Interface endpoints reach only AWS services, not an external API," rebuts an option that does not exist in this card (no option mentions VPC interface endpoints), leaving a dangling reference from an earlier version.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence about interface endpoints, or add a distractor that proposes VPC interface endpoints for reaching the payment API.

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: it describes AWS Lake Formation (S3 registration, Glue Data Catalog, LF-Tags, row/cell filters) while the question asks which of Lambda or Fargate runs a bursty API, a 40-minute nightly report, an S3-triggered thumbnailer and a 200,000-message queue, and what shortens cold starts. A learner would be taught a wholly wrong answer, and no part of the answer side covers the Lambda-vs-Fargate assignment.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the correct answer, e.g.: "Lambda for the bursty API (event-driven scaling, sub-second billing), the S3-triggered thumbnailer and the 200,000-message SQS queue (event source mapping scales consumers); Fargate for the nightly 40-minute report because Lambda's maximum execution time is 15 minutes. Shorten cold starts with provisioned concurrency (or SnapStart for supported runtimes), smaller deployment packages/fewer dependencies, higher memory (more CPU during init), and by creating SDK clients and DB connections outside the handler so they are reused by warm invocations."

findings.message: The keyed option names a specific setting, `strictAllowlist`, alongside `sandbox.network.allowedDomains`; the allowedDomains key is well established but the `strictAllowlist` flag is not something I can confirm in current Claude Code sandbox configuration, and a learner may copy it verbatim into settings.json.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the exact sandbox network setting names against current Claude Code documentation; if `strictAllowlist` is not a real key, reword the option to e.g. "Enable the Bash sandbox with network isolation and list only the few required domains in sandbox.network.allowedDomains (default-deny for everything else)."

findings.message: The parenthetical in "each at most 10 MB base64 and 8000 by 8000 px (5 MB on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud)" is attached to the pixel dimensions, so it reads as if Bedrock/Vertex have a 5 MB dimension limit rather than a smaller per-image byte limit.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "each image at most 10 MB on the Claude API (5 MB on Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI) and at most 8000 by 8000 px".

findings.message: The specific figures "up to 600 images per request (100 on 200k-context models)" and "10 MB base64 per image" should be re-verified against current Anthropic vision/limits documentation, since published guidance has previously stated a lower per-image size and a 100-image cap for API requests; these numbers are the core of the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Confirm the per-request image count and per-image size limits against the current Claude API vision documentation and restate them with the documented values (and keep the "as of" date in sync).

findings.message: The explanation rebuts an option that does not exist on the card: it says "self-managed Kafka on EC2 keeps the operational burden of sizing and patching brokers," but the only options are MSK Serverless, Kinesis Data Streams, Firehose and Amazon MQ. This will confuse a learner looking for that choice.
findings.suggestedFix: Either drop the "self-managed Kafka on EC2" sentence from the explanation, or add a fifth option such as "Run self-managed Apache Kafka brokers on Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups" with a matching "why".

findings.message: Option C (Amazon Data Firehose delivering to S3) is not a message broker at all and shares no protocol or consumer-group semantics with Kafka, so no learner working a Kafka-compatibility question would select it.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C with a closer-but-wrong choice, e.g. "Create a provisioned Amazon MSK cluster and size the broker instances for the 150 MB/s peak" (Kafka-compatible but requires broker sizing, so it fails the 'nobody wants to size brokers' requirement).

findings.message: Option b is the only option scoped specifically to the IoT/sensor-reading feature (c and f address only the traversal; d and e say "both features"), so in a Choose-two structure a learner who recognises that the two features need separate engines can key b by elimination without knowing anything about time-series databases.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a per-feature distractor for the IoT half, e.g. "Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with time-partitioned tables and a purge job for the sensor readings", with a why explaining that manual partitioning and retention jobs are exactly what a purpose-built time-series engine removes.

findings.message: Option D repeats option A verbatim (Firehose to S3 with multi-megabyte buffering) plus a trivial extra sentence about a runbook, so it is just as correct as the keyed option A and a learner cannot choose a single answer. Its "why" text discusses S3 Transfer Acceleration, which the option never mentions, indicating the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Restore the intended distractor for option D, e.g. "Keep one PutObject per reading but enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.", which matches the existing "why" and the explanation's list of rejected options.

findings.message: The stem's "Hint:" is a verbatim copy of the explanation's first sentence, so it already answers two of the three things the question asks (where the definition lives and which frontmatter fields are required) before the learner recalls anything.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop the hint, or replace it with a non-answering cue such as "Hint: think about file location, the fields Claude reads to decide delegation, and what context is (and is not) inherited."

findings.message: The explanation lists "fable" as a valid value for the agent frontmatter `model` field alongside sonnet/opus/haiku/inherit; this is not a recognised Claude model alias and looks like a typo or fabrication that would teach a wrong configuration value.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the supported `model` values against current Claude Code documentation and remove "fable" unless it is documented (e.g. "model can be sonnet, opus, haiku, a full model id, or inherit").

findings.message: Internal numeric inconsistency: the stem states a typical session runs 30 searches before the context fills, but option d's "why" says "after 25 bloated results have already cost money."
findings.suggestedFix: Change option d's rationale to "...after 30 bloated results have already cost money and attention..." to match the stem.

findings.message: Option C cites a `/autocompact` slash command; auto-compaction in Claude Code is controlled via settings/`/config` (with `/compact` for manual compaction), so the command name should be verified against current documentation before publishing.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword option C to avoid an unverified command name, e.g. "Raise the auto-compact threshold in settings so the large file fits comfortably."

findings.message: For REST APIs a VPC link private integration targets a Network Load Balancer only; Application Load Balancer (and Cloud Map) targets are supported by HTTP API VPC links, not REST API VPC links. The stem's "service behind an internal ALB" therefore cannot be reached directly by a REST API VPC link, so the explanation teaches a false mapping.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the explanation to: "A REST API private integration uses a VPC link to an internal Network Load Balancer; to front an internal ALB from a REST API, put an NLB in front of the ALB (or use an HTTP API, whose VPC links support ALB, NLB and Cloud Map)." Adjust the stem accordingly.

findings.message: The claim that the 29-second integration timeout "is a hard limit that no API type can raise" is no longer true: since mid-2024 the integration timeout quota for Regional and private REST APIs can be increased above 29 seconds via a service quota increase request (at the cost of reduced account-level throughput).
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "The integration timeout defaults to 29 seconds (50 ms minimum). For Regional and private REST APIs the 29-second limit can be raised by requesting a service quota increase, but the recommended pattern for a two-minute job is still to return 202 and complete the work asynchronously via SQS or Step Functions."

findings.message: The explanation rebuts an option that does not exist on the card: it says "Snowball is offline bulk transfer with no change capture, so it cannot support a near-zero cutover," but there is no AWS Snowball/Snow Family option among a-d. This leaves the learner looking for a fifth choice.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the trailing clause "; Snowball is offline bulk transfer with no change capture, so it cannot support a near-zero cutover" from the explanation (or add a Snow Family distractor as option e).

findings.message: Option C also satisfies every stated requirement: swapping the base64 bytes for a `url` source keeps the photo in the model's context and removes the 6 MB payload from every request, so p95 latency drops. Its "why" rejects it only because the photos are "confidential" and publicly hosting them is unacceptable — a constraint the stem never states — leaving two defensible answers.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the missing constraint to the stem, e.g. "...exchanges 40 tool-use turns about it. The inspection photos are confidential and must not be reachable from a public URL. Every request now carries the photo again and p95 latency has doubled. Which change fixes this while keeping the photo in the model's context?"

findings.message: The premise of a 6 MB photo being re-sent as base64 conflicts with the documented per-image size limit for inline image blocks (~5 MB per image; base64 encoding adds ~33% more), so the described starting state would be rejected by the API. Please re-check the current image-size limit and adjust the number.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a size that is valid inline, e.g. "receives a 4 MB photo", or state that the image is split/compressed to fit the inline limit before the base64 repetition is described.

findings.message: Option D's "why" asserts that "SSE-C has been blocked by default on new buckets since April 2026" — a specific, dated claim that is not needed to reject the option (SSE-C already fails the KMS-audit and key-revocation requirements) and that I cannot confirm against AWS documentation. If inaccurate it teaches a false fact about S3 defaults.
findings.suggestedFix: Either drop the last clause or re-verify it against current S3 documentation, e.g. end the why at "...there is no KMS Decrypt audit entry, and key material never reaches a service you can audit or revoke."

findings.message: The explanation credits the per-request usage object with "request-level cache and thinking detail," but the usage object exposes input, cache_creation, cache_read and output token counts only — extended thinking tokens are folded into output_tokens and are not reported as a separate field (as the keyed option b itself lists).
findings.suggestedFix: Change to "...with per-request usage logging for request-level cache-hit detail (cache creation vs. cache read tokens); thinking tokens are billed inside output_tokens."

findings.message: The explanation states that all role sessions, including AssumeRole, "carry no MFA information, so the key reads false." That is only true for sessions with no MFA in the authentication chain (EC2 instance profiles, Lambda execution roles, plain AssumeRole). When AssumeRole is called with --serial-number/--token-code (or from an MFA-validated session), the resulting role session does carry MFA context and aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent evaluates to true, which is exactly why MFA conditions can be enforced on human role sessions. As written, a learner would conclude MFA conditions can never be evaluated inside a role session.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "The trap: sessions with no MFA in their authentication chain (EC2 instance profiles, Lambda execution roles, plain AssumeRole calls) report aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent as false, so an MFA Deny in an SCP blocks every workload role. A role assumed with SerialNumber/TokenCode does carry MFA context (the key is true); still, put the MFA condition on the human role's trust policy rather than in an org-wide SCP."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: it describes Amazon SQS long polling (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds/WaitTimeSeconds, short vs. long polling, visibility timeout), while the question asks which AWS service runs Android device and Selenium desktop-browser tests on real hardware and what it is not built for. A learner would be taught a completely wrong answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with AWS Device Farm content, e.g.: "AWS Device Farm runs automated and manual tests on real, cloud-hosted mobile devices (physical Android and iOS phones and tablets) and on real desktop browsers via its Selenium-compatible desktop browser testing feature, returning videos, logs and performance data per device. It is not a load- or performance-testing service for your backend — generating synthetic traffic against an application is the job of a load testing tool (e.g. Distributed Load Testing on AWS), not Device Farm."

findings.message: The explanation presents the organizational view as simply available alongside the free account and public views, but AWS requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan to use the AWS Health API and its organizational view feature — so learners could conclude cross-account aggregation is available on Basic/Developer support.
findings.suggestedFix: Note the support-plan requirement for the organizational view, e.g. "organizational view (requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan) with a delegated administrator aggregates events across every account in AWS Organizations".

findings.message: The support-plan list for the AWS Health API ("Business Support+, Enterprise or Unified Operations plan") uses non-standard naming and omits Enterprise On-Ramp; the "Unified Operations" plan name cannot be confirmed against documented AWS Support tiers and should be re-checked.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-verify the current AWS Support plan names in AWS documentation and state them exactly, e.g. "the AWS Health API for programmatic polling requires a Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, or Enterprise Support plan."

findings.message: The card keys option d ("Compare published benchmark scores and pick the higher one") as correct, but its own "why" text explains why that approach is wrong, and the explanation endorses measuring dollars per completed task on a hard-task sample — which is option a. The keyed answer teaches a false method; option a is the correct one and is the only option with a null "why", confirming it was authored as the intended key.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option a and "correct": false on option d, move d's current text into its "why" role as a distractor rationale, and give option a a null/explanatory "why" consistent with the other correct-option convention.

findings.message: The explanation rebuts an option that does not exist in this card: "Kinesis Data Streams is a replayable ordered stream, not a work queue that hides and deletes items" — no option mentions Kinesis. This leftover text will confuse learners looking for the option it refers to.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the Kinesis clause (or replace it with the CPU-scaling rebuttal that matches option d), e.g. end with: "Synchronous calls and SNS push have no buffer, and average CPU lags the backlog, so neither keeps up with a spike."

findings.message: The scenario says uploads are "sometimes lost or processed twice," but the keyed option only addresses loss (delete-after-success plus DLQ); SQS standard queues remain at-least-once, so duplicates persist. Only the explanation mentions that consumers must be idempotent, so the keyed design as written does not fix the second symptom named in the stem.
findings.suggestedFix: Add idempotency to the keyed option text (e.g. "...delete a message only after the resize succeeds and make the resize idempotent (key the output object by image ID) so a redelivered message cannot corrupt results...") or drop "or processed twice" from the stem.

findings.message: The keyed option tells the learner to set "model": "claude-3-opus-20240229" — a Claude 3 Opus snapshot that Anthropic has deprecated and retired, so it would no longer be a usable value as of the review date (and it is inconsistent with the stem's current-generation "claude-sonnet-5" project setting).
findings.suggestedFix: Use a current Opus identifier in the keyed option, e.g. 'Add "model": "claude-opus-5" to .claude/settings.local.json in the repository.' (or the "opus" alias).

findings.message: Option D contains exactly the same configuration as the keyed option A ("Add Read(**/.env) and Read(**/.env.*) deny rules to permissions.deny in the shared .claude/settings.json") plus a purely administrative step, so it satisfies every stated requirement just as well as A; a learner cannot choose between them.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option D with a genuinely inferior alternative, e.g. "Add Edit(**/.env) and Edit(**/.env.*) deny rules to permissions.deny so the files cannot be modified." — which matches the existing "why" text about Edit-only rules.

findings.message: Option D's "why" explains why an Edit-only deny rule is insufficient, but the option text contains Read deny rules, not Edit rules; the rationale does not describe the option it is attached to (and the explanation likewise refers to a nonexistent "Edit-only" distractor).
findings.suggestedFix: Align option D's text with its "why" (make it an Edit-only deny rule), or rewrite the "why" to match whatever replacement text option D receives.

findings.message: The card's central claim that "a Read deny also blocks Edit and Write on the same path" is what makes a Read-only deny rule sufficient for the stem's "unable to read or overwrite" requirement; Claude Code's permission docs have historically documented Read(...) and Edit(...) as separate rule scopes. Re-verify this precedence against current documentation, since the keyed answer fails the overwrite half of the requirement if it is not true.
findings.suggestedFix: Confirm the Read-deny-implies-Edit/Write-deny behavior in current Claude Code permission docs; if it does not hold, change the keyed option to deny both Read(**/.env*) and Edit(**/.env*) and update the explanation accordingly.

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available," but nothing in the card ranks options by availability: the explanation and every distractor "why" argue cost per GB-month, retrieval fees and provisioned size, and the keyed option even adds a lifecycle transition to S3 Standard-IA, whose availability SLA (99.9%) is lower than S3 Standard's (99.99%). Option B's EFS Regional file system is multi-AZ with a 99.99% availability SLA, so it satisfies the stated qualifier at least as well as the key.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the qualifier with the card's reasoning and topic (4.1 Cost-optimized storage): change the stem to "Which storage service is the MOST cost-effective home for this library?" and keep the cost-based "why" texts. If availability is truly the intended axis, rewrite the options and explanation around durability/availability SLAs and drop the Standard-IA lifecycle from the keyed option.

findings.message: The keyed option A has "why": null while the other options have explanatory text; the keyed answer's rationale lives only in the shared explanation, which is inconsistent with the card's own pattern.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a short "why" to option A summarizing why S3 Standard (plus lifecycle and CloudFront) is the best fit for whole-object PUT/GET workloads.

findings.message: The code snippet sets output_config.effort on "claude-3-opus-20240229", but the card's own explanation lists effort support only for Fable 5.1, Opus 5/4.8/4.7/4.6, Sonnet 5/4.6 — a legacy Claude 3 model (retired well before the review date) does not accept the effort parameter, so the example teaches an invalid request.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the snippet's "model" to a model the explanation says supports all five levels, e.g. "claude-opus-5" (or "claude-sonnet-5").

findings.message: The stem asks for "the two consequences of changing effort mid-session," but the explanation names only one (changing the top-level value restarts the prompt cache); no second consequence is stated, so the learner cannot self-grade that part.
findings.suggestedFix: Either state both consequences explicitly (e.g. "1) the prompt cache is invalidated and must be rebuilt; 2) tool-calling behaviour/verbosity shifts for all subsequent output tokens") or reword the stem to ask for "the consequence of changing effort mid-session."

findings.message: The card's central numbers — a 600-page-per-request limit on 1M-context models and a 100-page limit on 200k-context models (option c's "why") — are the pivot of the keyed answer but are stated without a source; published PDF limits for the Messages API have historically been 100 pages/32MB per request. The author should confirm the 600/100 page figures against current Anthropic PDF-support documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a source citation to the Anthropic PDF support docs (page-limit table) and verify the 600-page (1M context) and 100-page (200k context) values, updating the stem, key and option c's "why" if the documented limits differ.

findings.message: Option c ("Switch to the largest available model") is ruled out directly by the stem's explicit constraint "without changing the model," so no attentive learner would consider it, and its "why" never mentions that it violates that stated constraint.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option c with a plausible non-model change, e.g. "Set a per-run token/cost budget in the API request and let the loop continue until the budget is exhausted," and have its "why" explain that a budget bounds spend but not iteration count or completion. If c is kept, amend its "why" to start with "The stem forbids changing the model...".

findings.message: The explanation concedes that AWS Snowball Edge is no longer offered to new customers (pointing them to DataSync, AWS Data Transfer Terminal or partners), yet the keyed answer instructs the learner to order Snowball Edge devices — so the card teaches a solution it simultaneously says may be unorderable. This availability claim and the keyed answer should be re-checked against current AWS Snow Family documentation as of the review date.
findings.suggestedFix: Either re-key/reword the correct option to a currently orderable offline transfer path (e.g. 'Use an AWS offline data transfer option such as AWS Data Transfer Terminal / Snow Family devices to copy the archive locally and ship it to AWS'), or move the availability caveat into the stem so the learner knows the question is testing the legacy exam rule.

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST cost-effective", but nothing in the card ranks options by cost: the explanation and every distractor "why" argue access control / tenant isolation ("a prompt is not an access control", "does nothing about workspace-wide visibility"). On cost grounds the keyed option (per-tenant workspaces plus a custom authorization layer) is arguably the most expensive, so the qualifier does not select it.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the qualifier and stem to the criterion actually being tested, e.g. qualifier "MOST secure" and stem "...Which design correctly isolates tenants' files?"

findings.message: Option d ("Delete every file immediately after each request") is not a design a learner would plausibly choose, since it neither addresses the client-supplied file_id problem nor workspace visibility, and its own "why" concedes it is merely symptomatic.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a more tempting but wrong option, e.g. "Store files with tenant-prefixed filenames and validate the prefix returned by the Files API before use."

findings.message: The explanation asserts "AWS no longer offers Snow devices to new customers" while the card keys "Order three Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices" as a correct action, which leaves the learner with a solution the card itself says cannot be ordered; the availability claim (and the 210 TB per-device capacity) should be re-verified against current AWS Snow Family documentation.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the current Snow Family availability and capacity statements, and if devices are genuinely unavailable to new customers, say so explicitly as an exam-only caveat (e.g. "Snow ordering is restricted today; the exam still keys the offline-shipping pattern, so learn the rule and use it only in exam scenarios") rather than as an aside that contradicts the keyed action.

findings.message: The card assumes aws:ResourceTag/project matching works uniformly for EC2, RDS and S3, but S3 bucket-level actions have historically had limited support for tag-based authorization (object-level ABAC uses s3:ExistingObjectTag, and bucket tags were not usable in authorization conditions). The author should verify against current S3 documentation whether aws:ResourceTag is supported for the bucket/object actions engineers need, since the explanation itself notes ABAC fails where a service does not support resource tags in authorization.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check current S3 documentation for aws:ResourceTag support on bucket-level actions; if support is still partial, note in the explanation that S3 access may need s3:ExistingObjectTag/prefix or access-point scoping alongside the tag-matching policy.

findings.message: Option e (client began logging the request-id response header) is a pure no-op that no learner would plausibly select as a cause of cache invalidation, since it touches only response handling and not the request at all.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option e with a plausible near-miss, e.g. "A `cache_control` breakpoint was moved from the last tool to the end of the system prompt" or "The request now sets a different `temperature` value", and give it a `why` explaining why it does or does not affect the cached prefix.

findings.message: The stem's qualifier "LOWEST cost" is not what separates the options: SCPs and IAM policies are both free, so cost only rules out the Config-rule option, and the real deciding criterion in the explanation and the "why" texts is preventive, non-removable enforcement. The qualifier is decorative and could mislead a learner into reasoning about price.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the qualifier with one that matches the actual discriminator, e.g. "Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?" or simply "Which solution meets these requirements?", and update mcq.qualifier accordingly.

findings.message: The stem itself ends with "Hint: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key.", which is verbatim the answer given in the explanation, so a learner who knows nothing about S3 encryption can produce the keyed answer from the question text alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the "Hint: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key." line from the question, or replace it with a non-revealing prompt such as "Hint: consider which option logs key usage in CloudTrail and what it costs per request."

findings.message: The realWorldUsage claim that S3 server access log destination buckets must stay on SSE-S3 is no longer accurate: Amazon S3 server access logging supports SSE-KMS-encrypted destination buckets provided S3 Bucket Keys are enabled on the destination bucket.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "If the destination bucket for S3 server access logs uses SSE-KMS, enable S3 Bucket Keys on that bucket — log delivery to an SSE-KMS bucket is only supported with Bucket Keys enabled (SSE-S3 always works)."

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST cost-effective", but the card decides the answer purely on security grounds: the explanation and every "why" argue about bounding destinations and residual exfiltration risk, never about cost. On the stated cost criterion option D (lowering max_content_tokens) is the option that most directly reduces spend, so the qualifier does not select the keyed answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the qualifier with a security one, e.g. stem: "Which configuration MOST effectively limits exfiltration risk while keeping the feature?" and set "qualifier" to "MOST effective at limiting exfiltration".

findings.message: Option b is the only option that carries its own justification ("because on Foundry the model parameter is the deployment name, which only defaults to the model ID"), while a, c and d are terse directives; this length/self-explanation asymmetry gives a test-wise learner a surface cue toward the key.
findings.suggestedFix: Trim option b to match the other options' style, e.g. "Send the deployment name the admin chose in the Foundry portal instead of the model ID.", and keep the reasoning in the explanation field.

findings.message: Option d is implausible on two counts: the scenario never mentions an Application Load Balancer at all, and for ALBs cross-zone load balancing is enabled by default and cannot be turned off at the load balancer level, so "enable" it is a no-op no learner would select as a cost fix.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d with a plausible but wrong cost lever tied to the scenario, e.g. "Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in each private subnet so traffic leaves the NAT gateway" (wrong because interface endpoints carry hourly and per-GB fees while the S3 gateway endpoint is free), and update its "why" accordingly.

findings.message: The explanation states a Message Batch holds at most 10,000 requests or 32 MB, but the current Batch API limit is 100,000 requests or 256 MB — and the card contradicts itself, since 150,000 requests would need 15 batches at 10,000 each, yet the explanation says "two batches" and realWorldUsage says to "split into 100,000-request batches".
findings.suggestedFix: Change to: "A Message Batch holds at most 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first, so 150,000 requests needs two batches."

findings.message: The stated Fargate ephemeral storage limit is wrong: since platform version 1.4.0 a Fargate task gets 20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default and can request up to 200 GiB via the task definition's ephemeralStorage parameter (Linux; 20 GiB fixed for Windows). Teaching "10 GiB ... with no option to request more" as a hard limit is false and describes pre-2020 behaviour.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with: "get 20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default on Linux tasks, expandable up to 200 GiB with the ephemeralStorage task definition parameter (platform version 1.4.0+)".

findings.message: The maximum task size "32 vCPU with 244 GB" does not match the documented Fargate task CPU/memory combinations, whose top tier is 16 vCPU with up to 120 GB (memory in 8 GB increments); 244 GB is not a valid Fargate memory value.
findings.suggestedFix: Re-check the current Fargate task size table and state the documented maximum (16 vCPU / 120 GB unless AWS has published a higher tier, in which case use the exact documented CPU/memory pair).

findings.message: "the SDK in the container uses the task role exclusively" is only true when a task role is defined; on the EC2 launch type a task with no taskRoleArn falls back to the container instance's instance profile credentials, which is precisely the trap the card warns about.
findings.suggestedFix: Clarify: "when a task role is set, the SDK in the container uses it instead of the instance profile; if you omit the task role on EC2, the container falls back to the instance profile credentials."

findings.message: Option b restates option a verbatim ("Save it as a skill in .claude/skills/backfill/SKILL.md with a one-line description.") and only adds an unrelated bookkeeping step, so it satisfies the LEAST-context-overhead qualifier exactly as well as the keyed option a; a learner cannot pick a single answer. The mismatch is confirmed by b's "why" (which argues about CLAUDE.md) and by the explanation, which says "CLAUDE.md, an unscoped rule and a SessionStart hook" are the three wrong choices — so b was evidently meant to be a CLAUDE.md option.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option b's text with the intended distractor, e.g. "Append the 300-line procedure to .claude/CLAUDE.md so it is always available.", keeping its existing "why".

findings.message: The explanation's claim that an interface endpoint is "dearer at near-zero traffic" than NAT is not true per endpoint: an interface endpoint costs $0.01 per AZ-hour versus $0.045 per AZ-hour for a NAT Gateway, so it is cheaper on fixed cost too; NAT only wins once you need roughly five or more interface endpoints per AZ. The deciding factor is the number of endpoints, not the traffic volume.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to: "an interface endpoint costs $0.01 per AZ-hour plus $0.01 per GB, so it beats NAT on both hourly and per-GB rates, but once each of dozens of VPCs needs several endpoints in every AZ the fixed hourly cost multiplies — hence centralise interface endpoints in one shared VPC reached through Transit Gateway and a Route 53 private hosted zone."

findings.message: The explanation ends with "the distractor is an interface endpoint for S3", but this is a question-and-answer card (mcq is null) with no options, so there is no distractor for the learner to see — the sentence is leftover MCQ text and is confusing as written.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a direct statement, e.g. "Note: an interface endpoint for S3 is not needed here — the free gateway endpoint covers in-Region, in-VPC S3 traffic; use an S3 interface endpoint only when access must come from on-premises or a peered VPC."

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"An AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint backed by the S3 ...\"", which quotes the keyed option verbatim, so a learner with no knowledge of the topic can pick option A from the stem alone.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint: ..." line from the question so the stem ends at "Which design meets this with the LEAST operational overhead?".

findings.message: Option d is word-for-word identical to the keyed option b, with only the harmless addition "Record the change in the team's runbook." Since d describes the same safeguard, it is equally correct and a learner cannot pick a single answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option d with a genuinely different, wrong safeguard — e.g. "Add a retry loop that resubmits every errored request in a second batch after the first batch ends."

findings.message: Option d's "why" talks about "discarding errors" hiding "the 30% of documents that were never processed," which has nothing to do with the option text (a pre-submit dry run plus a runbook entry); it fails to explain why the option is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Rewrite the "why" so it matches the replacement option text, e.g. explain that retrying after the batch ends still costs a full 20-hour run before the bug is detected.

findings.message: The keying is inverted: option B (cross-Region read replica / pilot light) is marked correct, yet its own "why" text explains why it is a poor fit, and the explanation plus realWorldUsage both argue that the backup-and-restore approach in option A (AWS Backup daily, cross-Region recovery-point copies, CloudFormation redeploy) is the MOST cost-effective answer for a 24-hour RPO/RTO. As keyed, the card teaches learners to pay for an always-on replica they do not need.
findings.suggestedFix: Set "correct": true on option A and "correct": false on option B; move option B's existing rejection text into its "why" field (it already reads as a distractor rationale) and leave option A's "why" as null.

findings.message: Option C is word-for-word identical to the keyed option A (only prefixed with "Proceed as follows:"), so two options state the same correct approach and a learner cannot pick a single answer. Option C's "why" (about mass re-encryption) does not match its text at all, indicating the intended distractor text was lost.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace option C's text with the re-encryption distractor its "why" describes, e.g. "For both keys, create a replacement key each year and re-encrypt all existing ciphertext and re-sign all artifacts under the new key, then delete the old key."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: it describes `disable_parallel_tool_use` inside `tool_choice`, while the question asks about the isolation boundary for Files API uploads and what should change. A learner is given a factually unrelated answer and learns nothing true about file scoping.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with the correct answer, e.g.: "Files uploaded via the Files API are scoped to the workspace, not to the API key. Every API key in the Default Workspace can list, retrieve and delete every file in that workspace, so one key per customer provides no isolation. The fix is to create a separate workspace per tenant (or per isolation domain) and issue that tenant's API keys from it, so file IDs from one tenant are inaccessible to another."

findings.message: The stem ends with "Hint: the correct option begins \"Upload each screenshot once to the Files API and reference ...\"", which quotes the keyed option (a) verbatim, so a learner with no knowledge of the topic can pick it with certainty.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the entire "Hint: ..." line from the question stem, leaving: "...Which change is MOST effective at keeping requests small without losing earlier screenshots?"

findings.message: The explanation's final sentence ("A bucket cannot hold an ACM certificate; S3 already terminates TLS with its own.") rebuts an option that does not exist in this card — no option mentions ACM or certificates — so it is a leftover that will confuse learners.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence "A bucket cannot hold an ACM certificate; S3 already terminates TLS with its own." (or add a matching ACM-certificate distractor if that rebuttal is intended).

findings.message: The stem's qualifier is "MOST highly available", but the keyed answer and every "why" (and the explanation and realWorldUsage) are argued purely on cost — nothing in the card ranks the options by availability, and a single lightly-used internet link plus one on-premises DataSync agent is not more highly available than a dedicated Direct Connect (which AWS would pair with an internet or second-connection backup) or a managed Transfer Family endpoint. The topic ("Cost-optimized storage") and stableUid ("lowest-cost-transfer-into-aws") confirm the intended qualifier was cost.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the stem to "Which solution transfers the nightly data at the LOWEST cost?" and set mcq.qualifier to "LOWEST cost" so the keyed DataSync option and the cost-based "why" texts match the qualifier.

findings.message: Option C (using Amazon Transcribe's transcript confidence scores to infer customer mood) is implausible on two counts at once — the input is explicitly free text, not audio, and confidence scores are obviously not a sentiment signal — so no learner would seriously consider it.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a plausible-but-wrong managed-AI option, e.g. "Call Amazon Comprehend's DetectKeyPhrases API and route tickets based on which key phrases appear" (wrong because key phrases do not yield a positive/negative/neutral/mixed label).

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the question at all: the stem asks about federation paths (Okta SSO across many accounts, a standalone account, mobile app end-users uploading to S3) and where IAM users are still appropriate, but the explanation text is entirely about Lambda invocation retry behaviour, async queues, DLQs and destinations. A learner would be taught nothing correct about the asked topic.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with content matching the stem, e.g.: "Dozens of accounts under AWS Organizations: use IAM Identity Center with Okta as the external SAML/SCIM identity provider, assigning permission sets that provision roles in each member account. The single standalone account: use direct SAML 2.0 (or OIDC) federation to an IAM role via an IAM identity provider, or add the account to Organizations and use Identity Center. Mobile app customers: use Amazon Cognito identity pools to exchange a user pool (or social) token for temporary credentials scoped to a prefix in the S3 bucket - never embed long-lived keys in the app. IAM users remain appropriate only for the few cases without federation support: service or emergency break-glass access, and even then prefer IAM Roles Anywhere or access keys rotated and guarded by MFA."

findings.message: The explanation does not answer the stem at all: the question asks about S3 Cross-Region Replication (versioning prerequisites, why existing objects are not replicated, and CRR's place among replication mechanisms), but the explanation describes AWS Application Migration Service, Application Discovery Service, Migration Hub and DMS. A learner would be taught content unrelated to (and therefore wrong for) the asked question.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the explanation with an answer to the stem, e.g.: "Both the source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled, and S3 needs an IAM role with permission to read from the source and replicate into the destination. Enabling CRR only replicates objects created or updated after the rule is added, so last year's existing objects are not copied; use S3 Batch Replication (an S3 Batch Operations job) to backfill them. CRR is one of two S3 Replication flavours - CRR across Regions and SRR within a Region - configured per bucket via replication rules, and it is asynchronous, so it is not a substitute for synchronous durability mechanisms."

findings.message: The stem bundles three independent questions (bucket prerequisites, why CRR alone is insufficient, and CRR's position among AWS replication mechanisms), so the learner cannot self-grade a single recall target.
findings.suggestedFix: Split into separate cards, or narrow the stem to one ask, e.g.: "A compliance rule requires copies of a bucket's objects in a second Region, including objects uploaded last year. What must be true of both buckets, and why does enabling CRR alone not satisfy the rule?"
